summary: Describes the relational extension to Sieve, which lets tests use relational operators and test counts of entities in header and envelope fields as well as their content. It replaces RFC 3431. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: This lets a mail rule compare things, like is there more than three of something or is this value bigger.

questions: what is the sieve relational extension
sieve value vs count match type
subtitle: Lets Sieve mail filters compare values with greater-than and less-than, and count headers or addresses.

tldr.problem: The base Sieve language can only test whether a header or address matches a string. It cannot ask whether a value is bigger than another, or how many addresses a message has.
tldr.mechanism: The RELATIONAL extension adds two match types, :value and :count, that take one of six operators (gt, ge, lt, le, eq, ne). :value compares strings; :count compares the number of entities with a number.
tldr.outcome: A filter can now do things like file mail with an X-Priority below 3 into a Priority folder, or flag mail with more than 5 recipients. It is a Proposed Standard that replaces RFC 3431.

facts.label: Operators
facts.value: gt, ge, lt, le, eq, ne

today: RFC 5231 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2008. It obsoletes RFC 3431 and is not itself marked as obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What the Extension Adds
sections.content:
RFC 5231 defines the RELATIONAL extension to the Sieve mail filtering language. It gives the address, envelope and header tests relational operators, so a script can say that a field is greater than or less than a value instead of only equal to it.

The RFC gives two example uses. Messages whose x-priority field is greater than 3 can be moved to a 'work on later' folder, and mail can be sorted by the sender's userid, with names starting 'a' to 'm' going to one folder and the rest to another. A script can also count things, such as whether the to and cc fields hold more than 5 addresses.

The extension is switched on in a script with the capability string relational.
sections.eli5: Before, a mail rule could only ask 'is it exactly this?'. Now it can also ask 'is it more than this?' or 'how many are there?'.

sections.title: The VALUE and COUNT Match Types
sections.content:
The RFC defines two new match types. Each is a tag, :value or :count, followed by a quoted relational operator.

  • gt: greater than, like the C operator >
  • ge: greater than or equal
  • lt: less than
  • le: less than or equal
  • eq: equal to
  • ne: not equal to

For a relation, the value from the message is the left side. The value from the test's key list is the right side.
sections.eli5: There are six words for comparing, like 'bigger', 'smaller' and 'the same'. You say which one you want, then what to compare against.

sections.title: How VALUE Compares Strings
sections.content:
The VALUE match type does a relational comparison between strings. It may be used with any comparator that returns sort information.

If there are several values on either side or on both sides, the test is true if any pair satisfies the relation.
sections.eli5: If you give the rule a few things to check against, it passes when at least one of them works out.

sections.title: How COUNT Counts
sections.content:
The COUNT match type first works out how many of the named entities the message has. It then compares that number with the values in the test. It SHOULD only be used with numeric comparators.

  • The address test counts the mailbox elements defined in RFC 2822. Group names are ignored, but the mailboxes inside them are counted.
  • The envelope test counts addresses in the named envelope parts. Envelope to always has one entry, the user the script runs for. Envelope from counts 0 if MAIL FROM is empty and 1 otherwise.
  • The header test counts the total number of instances of the named fields. It does not count the individual addresses inside to, cc and similar fields.

When several field names are listed, their counts are added together. To compare counts separately, use two comparisons joined by allof or anyof.
sections.eli5: COUNT is like counting how many apples are in a basket and then asking if that number is big enough. If you name two baskets, you count both together.

sections.title: Comparators and Other Sieve Actions
sections.content:
The extension defines no comparators of its own. Any comparator used is treated as defined in the base Sieve specification. The i;ascii-numeric comparator from RFC 4790 MUST be supported by any implementation of this extension, and it MUST handle at least 32-bit unsigned integers. Larger integers MAY be supported, and the comparator does not support negative numbers.

There is no interaction with other Sieve operations or known extensions. In particular it has no effect on the implicit KEEP or on any explicit message action.
sections.eli5: Numbers are compared using a standard number-comparing rule that every mail filter with this feature has to know. It does not change what the filter does with your mail after it decides.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC uses a message with two received fields, a subject, a to field with two addresses and a cc field with one. Counting addresses across to and cc with ge 3 is true, because there are three. Counting to alone, or cc alone, against 3 is false.

Counting header instances works differently. received alone has 2 instances, so ge 3 is false, but received plus subject gives 3, so it is true. A header count over to and cc against 3 is always false on a compliant RFC 2822 message, since a message can have at most one of each field: it counts fields, not addresses.

The extended example in section 7 files mail with x-priority below 3 into Priority, mail with more than 5 to addresses into SPAM, and splits the rest by whether the sender sorts after 'M'. A final test files mail into Only me when the to and cc fields hold exactly one address and it is the user's own.
sections.eli5: The examples show that counting 'how many addresses' and counting 'how many lines of a type' give different answers, so you have to pick the right one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: An implementation MUST make sure the test for envelope to reflects only the delivery to the current user. A user must not be able to use this test to find out whether the message was also delivered to someone else. Further security considerations are in the base Sieve specification.
sections.eli5: A rule must not be able to peek at who else got the same message. It only sees your own copy.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 3431
sections.content: Apart from editorial changes, the notable changes are updated references, including moving the comparator reference from ACAP to RFC 4790, and updated and corrected examples. The ABNF gained definition comments for gt, lt and the rest, and the text now clarifies which RFC 2822 elements the COUNT test counts. The requirement to strip white space from header fields before comparing was removed, because a more general version was added to the base Sieve specification.
sections.eli5: This is a tidied-up second edition: clearer wording, fixed examples and newer references.
